## Global change impacts Earth's systems
<hr>
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>

<div style="float: left; width: 50%;">

**Earth's system's interact at the ecosystem level**

<br/>

<span style="color:darkred">**Ecosystem</span> = A community of living things interacting with each other and with the nonliving environment (like air, water, and soil).**

<br/>

**A change in just one <span style="color:blue">*biotic*</span> or <span style="color:blue">*abiotic*</span> factor can alter complex relationships and have large scale consequences**

</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:220px; LEFT:575px; WIDTH:450px; HEIGHT:450px" SRC="images/earthsystems.png">

## In ecosystems, abiotic and biotic processes interact
<hr>

<div style="float: left; width: 48%;">

**Ecosystems (and higher levels) are regulated by the <span style="color:darkred">flow of energy</span> and the <span style="color:darkred">cycling of nutrients</span>**

<br/>

**Life is composed of <span style="color:blue">energy</span> and <span style="color:blue">matter</span>, which is always on the move**

<br/>

- **Energy from the sun powers communities, ecosystems, biomes, etc**
    + energy in nature isn’t recycled — it flows one way
    
<br/>

- **Matter, including the chemical building blocks of life, cycles around the biosphere**
    + matter can’t be created or destroyed — it just changes form

</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:200px; LEFT:575px; WIDTH:500px; HEIGHT:450px" SRC="images/energymatter.jpg">

## Matter recycling: Water
<hr>

* **<span style="color:blue">Evaporation & Transpiration</span>: Water moves from land and plants into the atmosphere**
<br/>
* **<span style="color:blue">Precipitation</span>: Rain, snow, sleet, or hail falls to Earth**
<br/>
* **<span style="color:blue">Condensation</span>: Water vapor forms clouds**

<br/>
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>

* **<span style="color:blue">Infiltration & Runoff</span>: Water soaks into soils, feeds groundwater, or flows into rivers and streams**
<br/>
* **<span style="color:blue">Storage</span>: Water is stored in ice, snowpack, soils, wetlands, lakes, groundwater, and oceans until it re-enters the cycle**

    
</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:200px; LEFT:500px; WIDTH:550px; HEIGHT:375px" SRC="images/watercycle2.png">

## Matter recycling: Water
<hr>
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>

<div style="float: right; width: 48%;">

* **Role of mountain ecosystems in water cycle:**
    + Mountains store water in snowpack, bogs, soils, and forests
    + Mountain vegetation releases water vapor into the atmosphere
    + Moist air cools as it rises over mountains, increasing condensation
    
</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:220px; LEFT:30px; WIDTH:550px; HEIGHT:375px" SRC="images/watercycle2.png">

## Global change will alter most parts of the water cycle
<hr>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:160px; LEFT:150px; WIDTH:800px; HEIGHT:500px" SRC="images/waterchange.png">

## Matter recycling: Nutrients
<hr>

<span style="color:green">**Main Components of Nutrient Cycles (e.g., nitrogen, carbon, phosphorus, sulfur):**</span>

<div style="float: left; width: 48%;">

<br/>

**<span style="color:green">Inputs</span>: Nutrients enter ecosystems from weathering rocks, atmospheric deposits or biological capture**

<br/>

**<span style="color:green">Uptake</span>: Plants and microbes absorb nutrients to build living tissue**

<br/>

**<span style="color:green">Transfer</span>: Nutrients move through food webs as organisms eat and are eaten**

<br/>

**<span style="color:green">Decomposition & Recycling</span>: Dead matter and waste are broken down, returning nutrients to soil and water**

<br/>

**<span style="color:green">Storage</span>: Nutrients can be held long-term in soils, sediments, biomass, or rock until re-mobilized**

</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:200px; LEFT:600px; WIDTH:500px; HEIGHT:450px" SRC="images/nutrient.jpg">

## Matter recycling: Nutrients
<hr>

<div style="float: left; width: 50%;">

<span style="color:green">**Role of Mountain Ecosystems:**</span>

<br/>

**<span style="color:green">Sources</span>: Bedrock and soils release nutrients through weathering, feeding streams and forests**

<br/>

**<span style="color:green">Storage</span>: Soils, wetlands, and living biomass serve as major nutrient storage pools.**

<br/>

**<span style="color:green">Transfer</span>: Aquatic systems are often "throughput systems" where nutrients pass through quickly rather than being significantly retained**

<br/>

**<span style="color:green">Decomposition & Recycling</span>: Generally slower than in warmer lowland or tropical systems, meaning nutrients cycle gradually and can become limiting for growth**

</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:200px; LEFT:600px; WIDTH:500px; HEIGHT:450px" SRC="images/nutrient.jpg">

## Why care about Nitrogen?
<hr>
<br/>
<br/>

<div style="float: left; width: 48%;">

**Nitrogen is one of the fundamental building blocks for life on Earth, especially plants**

<br/>

- **Nitrogen is the limiting factor in how productive plant growth can be**
    + producers at bottom of food webs
    + human food security

<br/>

- **Thus, Nitrogen is a primary ingredient in fertilizers**

</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:220px; LEFT:570px; WIDTH:500px; HEIGHT:375px" SRC="images/plantnitro.png">

## Nitrogen cycle: the basics
<hr>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:180px; LEFT:200px; WIDTH:700px; HEIGHT:500px" SRC="images/nitrogencycle2.png">

## Global change will alter most parts of the nitrogen cycle
<hr>
<span style="color:red">**Not all the nutrients in fertilizers get absorbed by plants and the excess moves its way into rivers, lakes, oceans and groundwater as agricultural runoff**</span>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:215px; LEFT:125px; WIDTH:850px; HEIGHT:450px" SRC="images/reactivenitro.jpg">

## The state of nitrogen cycling in Appalachian ecosystems
<hr>
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>

<div style="float: left; width: 63%;">

* **Appalachian ecosystems are no longer under peak nitrogen stress thanks to air quality improvements (Clean Air Act 1990)**

<br/>

* **Legacies of past deposition, slow soil recovery, and climate-driven mobilization mean nitrogen cycling remains disrupted**
    + especially in high-elevation forests and sensitive headwater streams

</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:180px; LEFT:700px; WIDTH:350px; HEIGHT:500px" SRC="images/nitrogendeposit.png">

## The state of nitrogen cycling in Appalachian ecosystems
<hr>
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>

<div style="float: left; width: 49%;">


* **Appalachian agriculture creates a leaky nitrogen cycle (like most agriculture)**
    + farmland releases more nitrogen than natural mountain ecosystems
    + agriculture is a main driver of nitrogen pollution regionally and downstream

</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:180px; LEFT:500px; WIDTH:550px; HEIGHT:500px" SRC="images/nitrogenag.png">

## Why care about carbon?
<hr>

<div style="float: left; width: 52%;">

**Carbon is in carbon dioxide and methane, both greenhouse gases that trap heat close to Earth**

<br/>

- **Carbon is stored deep earth, vegetation and oceans for potentially long time scales**
    + keeps carbon out of atmosphere
 
<br/>
 
- **Human activities (burning fossil fuels, deforestation, agriculture) have added more carbon to the atmosphere than ecosystems can re-absorb**

<br/>

**Carbon footprint is used as shorthand for the amount of carbon being emitted by an activity or organization**

</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:180px; LEFT:575px; WIDTH:525px; HEIGHT:450px" SRC="images/carbonfootprint.jpg">

<hr>

## The state of carbon cycling in Appalachian ecosystems
<hr>
<div style="float: left; width: 52%;">

**<span style="color:purple">Forests as Carbon Sinks</span>: Appalachian forests are key carbon 'sinks', pulling CO₂ from the air and storing it in wood**

<br/>

**<span style="color:purple">Soil Carbon</span>: Cool, moist mountain soils store large pools of organic matter, but warming could accelerate decomposition and release carbon**

<br/>

**<span style="color:purple">Disturbance Impacts</span>: Past logging, mining, and land use change have reduced carbon stocks in some areas, though reforestation has helped recovery**

<br/>

**<span style="color:purple">Agriculture & Development</span>: Expanding agriculture and urban areas are net carbon 'sources', emitting more than they store**

</div>

<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:180px; LEFT:600px; WIDTH:475px; HEIGHT:450px" SRC="images/carbontree.png">

## Why does nutrient cycles matter, globally?
<hr>
<br/>
<br/>
<br/>

<div style="float: left; width: 50%;">

**Biochemical cycles interact to regulate the biosphere, including climate &#8594;**

<br/>

**Biogeochemistry is a foundation of biomes: living things adapted to a specific regions  &#8594;**

<br/>

**Ecosystems are the interactions with the biotic and abiotic within those regions**

</div>


<IMG STYLE="position:absolute; TOP:200px; LEFT:550px; WIDTH:550px; HEIGHT:400px" SRC="images/biomes.png">
